This post is about a contrast that the dose-response series has circled but never stated outright. Two drugs can act on the **same cell** — the microglia that drive the neuroinflammatory component of ME/CFS — through **different receptors**, and produce **opposite dose-response behaviour** in the same patient. One drug, taken at the top of its range, produced nothing for months. The other, taken at a fraction of a milligram, changed the patient's illness within days. That contrast is not noise. Read correctly, it is a differential diagnosis performed with a prescription pad.

The case is documented in the primary paper's microglial cascade and medication-response chapters [@Loth2026website]. What follows separates what the record actually shows from the interpretation layered on it — the same evidence-versus-model discipline the series has used throughout.

---

## The record

**LDN, at the top of its range, was a null.** Low-dose naltrexone was taken at 4–4.5 mg daily from February 2026. After roughly six months, the honest assessment was no clear net benefit — no improvement that clearly exceeded the illness's own fluctuation. Notably, the range below 4 mg — the 0.5–1.5 mg window where LDN's TLR4/Nrf2 mechanism is hypothesised to live — was never tested. The trial was a single point at the top of the dose range, held for six months. A follow-up clinical note explicitly flagged the open question: if non-response at 4 mg is confirmed, the distinct pharmacology of a ~1 mg trial remains untested.

**LDA, at a fraction of the antipsychotic dose, was a window.** Aripiprazole was started at 0.5 mg on 10 July 2026 and moved to 1 mg two days later. Within eight days the record showed: zero brain-fog episodes in eight days where they had been near-daily; normal concentration; and the sharpest edge of the contrast — before LDA, twenty minutes of moderate rowing reliably produced a nine-day post-exertional crash. On LDA, five hours of chainsaw work produced *no PEM at all*. The clinical note that documented this also recorded what did *not* respond: tinnitus persisted unchanged, vanishing only after nights of deep sleep and returning with fatigue.

Two results, same patient, same months, same underlying illness. The interpretive question is what the contrast means.

---

## What makes the contrast informative: two receptors on one cell

The reason this is more than anecdote is the target anatomy. LDN's proposed mechanism at low dose runs through **TLR4** on microglia — blocking a danger-signal receptor partially enough to trigger an Nrf2-mediated anti-inflammatory shift. LDA's mechanism runs through **D2/D3 receptors** on the same microglia — partially agonising a receptor whose engagement raises the activation threshold and suppresses cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6). Both receptors sit on the same cell population, engaged by two different molecules, and the paper's microglial cascade treats them as complementary probes of the same node: TLR4 antagonism removes one input among many; D2 agonism raises the threshold the inputs must cross [@Loth2026website].

Two probes of one cell can disagree in exactly two instructive ways.

**Pattern one: both work.** Microglial involvement confirmed; multi-receptor. Informative but not sharp.

**Pattern two: one is a null at its tested dose, the other opens a window.** This is the pattern the record shows, and it is sharper. The LDA window — complete PEM protection at 1 mg — says the microglial activation-threshold mechanism is real and *drug-accessible through D2* in this patient. The LDN null says only that the *tested dose* of LDN produced no net benefit — and here the dose discipline the series has built matters. The 4–4.5 mg trial sat at the top of the range, above the hypothesised TLR4/Nrf2 window and past the point where benefit is expected to extinguish. Under the non-propagation principle ([higher doses do not contain the benefits of lower ones](../concentration-not-presence/)), a null at 4.5 mg carries **no information about 1 mg**. The mechanism may be absent — or the trial may simply have never run the mechanism's window.

This is why the honest conclusion is asymmetric. The LDA result is *positive evidence*: a window opened at a mechanistically predicted dose. The LDN result is *absence of evidence at a dose where evidence was not expected* — a null that cannot exclude the mechanism, only the dose.

---

## The resistant domain is part of the signal

The tinnitus result belongs in the analysis, because it is what elevates the case from "LDA works" to "the model has structure." If LDA's benefit were a general blunting of symptoms — placebo, mood, energy — the tinnitus should have improved too. It did not, and its behaviour (worse with fatigue, clearing only after nights of deep sleep) points at a different mechanism entirely: thalamo-cortical sensory gating, a GABAergic/glutamatergic circuit with no dopamine handle for aripiprazole to grip. A drug that fully protects one layer and leaves a mechanistically distinct layer untouched is behaving like a *targeted* drug, not a general one. The domain dissociation is itself the evidence that the microglial/dopaminergic model is doing explanatory work — and the paper builds exactly this principle into its interpretation framework: a resistant domain identifies which symptoms share a pathway and which do not, without requiring a biomarker [@Loth2026website].

The corollary the record states explicitly is worth repeating, because it is the Goldilocks discipline applied to success: **do not raise the dose to chase the resistant domain.** The tinnitus is a target failure, not a dose failure. Escalating LDA past ~1.5–2 mg would not touch a GABAergic circuit — it would only walk the drug out of its own window and toward net D2 antagonism ([the partial-agonist flip](../low-dose-aripiprazole-window/)).

---

## What this pattern would mean as a general diagnostic

Generalised from one documented case, the pattern becomes a probe any patient and clinician already possess. The paper's combination-inference framework formalises it [@Loth2026website]:

- **LDA window + LDN window** → microglial involvement confirmed through both TLR4 and D2; treat neuroinflammation as a multi-input node.
- **LDA window + LDN null (within-range)** → D2 is the therapeutically accessible microglial receptor; TLR4 is not rate-limiting. This is the sharpest exclusion available.
- **LDN window + LDA null** → the reverse: TLR4 carries the microglial signal; D2 does not add.
- **Both null (both within-range)** → microglial activation may not be the rate-limiting node at all — the differential moves to autoantibodies, B-cell pathology, mast-cell-driven, or structural causes.

The load-bearing word in every row is *within-range*. The diagnostic power of the two-drug contrast exists only when each drug has actually been tried inside its own window. A null at the top of a dose range, as this patient's LDN history illustrates, is an open question — which is why the clinical note's own suggestion, a ~1 mg LDN trial, is not a retreat but the missing experiment.

---

## Certainty

| Claim | Certainty |
|-------|-----------|
| LDA at ~1 mg produced the documented PEM protection and domain dissociation | High as a reported observation — single patient, no control, natural fluctuation not fully excludable |
| The benefit runs through microglial D2 (not 5-HT1A or mesocorticolimbic D2) | Low — plausible and consistent with the domain pattern; not separately testable without a selective probe |
| The LDN 4–4.5 mg null says nothing about LDN at 0.5–1.5 mg | Moderate — follows from the occupancy model; empirically untested in this patient |
| The two-receptor pattern generalises as a diagnostic | Low — the combination-inference framework is mechanistically derived and prospectively untested |
